about: In the Lent and Easter terms of Cambridge Engineering Part IA, students do a programme of short (one 2-hour session) and long (lab session plus written report) experiments across mechanics, thermofluids, structures, materials and electrical and information engineering. They are credited as coursework under the standard credit system, with separate qualifying marks for the Mechanical, Structures and Materials, and Electrical and Information Engineering groups (2026–27 credit notice). The experiment list comes from the Part IA guide on the 2026–27 site, whose footer says it was last updated in 2022, so check it against this year's lab timetable. This guide explains the format, the rules that cost marks and the background theory for each experiment; it does not invent experiment content beyond the official titles.

notes.h: The Part IA experiments and how they are credited
notes.body:
In the Lent and Easter terms of Part IA, Cambridge engineers do a programme of laboratory experiments that back up the lecture courses examined in Papers 1–3. They are coursework, credited under the "standard credit" system, not a lecture course with its own exam.

The experiments listed in the Part IA guide (2026–27 site)
Warning: this list may be out of date. The guide's footer says it was last updated on 14 September 2022, the guide says students do 11 experiments while its table lists 12, and the 2026–27 credit notice includes a "blended" experiment that the list does not name. Use this year's lab timetable and Moodle as the authority.
Mechanics
- Measurement of vehicle motion (long)
- Vibration modes (short)
- Angular momentum (short)
Thermofluids
- Stirling engine (long)
- Turbocharger (short)
- Inviscid fluid flow (short)
Structures
- Elastic beams (long)
Materials
- Plasticity and fracture (long)
Electrical and information engineering
- Iron-cored transformer (short)
- AC power (short)
- Combinational logic (short)
- Sequential logic, memory and counting (short)

Short and long experiments
- A short experiment fills one 2-hour session and is completed and signed off in that session.
- A long experiment is 2 hours in the lab followed by a written report, which is marked by a demonstrator at a signing session.

How they are credited (2026–27 credit notice)
Experiments are grouped by subject, and each group has its own qualifying mark.
- Mechanical Engineering (Lent, Easter): 4 short experiments at 2 marks and 2 long experiments at 6 marks: 20 marks available, qualifying mark 14.
- Electrical and Information Engineering (Lent, Easter): 4 short experiments at 2 marks: 8 available, qualifying mark 8.
- Structures and Materials (Lent, Easter): 1 "blended" experiment at 3 marks and 2 long experiments at 6 marks: 15 available, qualifying mark 11. The guide's (2022) list does not name the blended experiment, so check the lab timetable and Moodle.
The Electrical and Information Engineering group has a qualifying mark equal to the maximum, so every one of those short experiments must be completed.

Marking scale (Part IA guide)
- A satisfactorily completed short experiment earns 2 marks.
- A long experiment is marked out of 6: 4 for completing it with minimally acceptable work, 5 for satisfactory work and 6 for exceptional work.

Standard credit
Once you reach the qualifying mark for a group, extra marks do not count; if you fall short, or fail to attend or hand in work, the shortfall comes off your Tripos total. Coursework as a whole is worth 100 of the 900 Part IA marks in 2026–27.

Exam tips: the experiments are not examined directly, but each one illustrates a Paper 1–3 topic; note down the link as you go.

notes.h: Lab books, long reports, deadlines and lateness
notes.body:
Most lost lab marks come from organisation, not physics. The Part IA guide sets out clear rules; the main ones are summarised here. The guide's footer says it was last updated in 2022, so always check this year's version of the rules on Moodle.

Before the session
- Check the lab chart so you know where your next experiment is.
- Read the online handout in advance (printed copies are also available in the lab).
- Bring your lab notebook to every long experiment, and your safety glasses (issued at the start of the year) to materials labs and structural design practicals. You may be excluded without them.

Timing and lateness
- Morning lab sessions start at 5 minutes past the hour; afternoon sessions start on the hour.
- Arriving up to 10 minutes late costs 1 mark, and the demonstrator may exclude you.
- Arriving more than 10 minutes late excludes you from a lab experiment.
- If you miss a session for reasons beyond your control, follow the Department's rearrangement procedure and talk to your Director of Studies or Tutor.

The lab record
- Record all readings, observations and calculations directly in the lab notebook, not on loose sheets. Glue or staple in any printed charts or word-processed pages.
- Start each experiment on a new page with a clear heading and the date.
- Plan your results tables before taking readings, with labelled columns and units.
- Plot graphs during the experiment where you can, so anything unexpected is spotted while you can still re-measure. Label axes and show the accuracy of the data.

Long reports
- The report goes in the lab notebook and is marked by a demonstrator (together with your partner's) at a signing session.
- The signing session must happen within 15 days of the experiment. You book it in a free period of the lab schedule.
- Late reports lose 1 mark for each week, or part of a week, that they are late.
- The Department's report-writing guidance and the Part IA Exposition classes explain what a good long report looks like.

Academic integrity
- Discussing the experiment with colleagues, demonstrators and supervisors is encouraged.
- The report itself must be your own work; the guide says copying the work of others is unacceptable.

Safety
The guide's lab rules include no eating or drinking in labs, following demonstrators' instructions, keeping loose clothing away from rotating machinery, not taking leads, components or equipment from other lab locations, and reporting any faults in the equipment you use.

Exam tips: a well-kept notebook doubles as revision notes; write one line per experiment on which lecture result it tests.

notes.h: Preparing for the experiments: background theory
notes.body:
Background theory (general background, not taken from the experiment handouts)
Each experiment title points to theory from a Part IA lecture course. The handouts define exactly what you measure and are the authority; the results below are standard textbook background, linked to the experiment titles only, that is worth revising before you go in.

Mechanics (Paper 1)
- Measurement of vehicle motion: displacement, velocity and acceleration are linked by differentiation, v = dx/dt and a = dv/dt. Differentiating measured data amplifies noise, so smoothing or fitting matters.
- Vibration modes: a system has natural frequencies and associated mode shapes; driving it near a natural frequency produces resonance. For a single mass on a spring, ωn = √(k/m).
- Angular momentum: with no external torque about an axis, angular momentum about that axis, H = Iω for a rigid body, is conserved.

Thermofluids (Paper 1)
- Stirling engine: the ideal Stirling cycle has two isothermal processes and two constant-volume processes. With a perfect regenerator its ideal efficiency equals the Carnot value, 1 − Tc/Th; real engines fall well short.
- Turbocharger: an exhaust-driven turbine powers a compressor on the same shaft. The steady-flow energy equation links work to changes in enthalpy.
- Inviscid fluid flow: along a streamline in steady, incompressible, inviscid flow, p + ½ρv² + ρgz is constant (Bernoulli).

Structures and Materials (Paper 2)
- Elastic beams: for elastic bending, σ/y = M/I = E/R, so stress grows linearly with distance from the neutral axis.
- Plasticity and fracture: a tensile test gives Young's modulus, yield (or 0.2% proof) strength, tensile strength and ductility. Ductile fracture follows necking and void growth; brittle fracture is sudden with little plastic deformation.

Electrical and Information Engineering (Paper 3)
- Iron-cored transformer: for an ideal transformer V1/V2 = N1/N2 and I1/I2 = N2/N1. Real transformers have winding (copper) losses, core losses from hysteresis and eddy currents (reduced by laminating the core), and draw a magnetising current.
- AC power: with rms voltage V and current I separated by phase angle φ, real power P = VI cos φ, reactive power Q = VI sin φ and apparent power S = VI, so S² = P² + Q². The power factor is cos φ.
- Combinational logic: outputs depend only on present inputs. De Morgan's theorems: NOT(A·B) = NOT A + NOT B, and NOT(A + B) = NOT A · NOT B. NAND (or NOR) gates alone can build any logic function.
- Sequential logic, memory and counting: outputs depend on stored state as well as inputs. Flip-flops store one bit; chaining them makes registers and counters, and n flip-flops can count through up to 2ⁿ states.

Worked example (AC power)
A load draws 5 A rms from a 230 V rms supply with power factor 0.8 lagging. S = 230 × 5 = 1150 VA, P = 1150 × 0.8 = 920 W and Q = √(1150² − 920²) = 690 var.

Exam tips: before each lab, write the governing equation at the top of the page and predict one number; the comparison between prediction and measurement is the heart of a good report.

questions.q: Under the Part IA guide's marking scale, a long experiment that is completed but only to a minimally acceptable standard earns:
questions.why: Long experiments are marked out of 6: 4 for completion with minimally acceptable work, 5 for satisfactory work and 6 for exceptional work. 2 marks is the credit for a satisfactorily completed short experiment.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has 1200 primary turns and 60 secondary turns. The primary is connected to 240 V rms and the secondary supplies 2 A rms to a resistive load. What is the primary current?
questions.why: The turns ratio is 20:1, so V2 = 240/20 = 12 V and, for an ideal transformer, I1 = I2 × N2/N1 = 2 × 60/1200 = 0.1 A. Check: 240 × 0.1 = 12 × 2 = 24 W. 40 A multiplies by the turns ratio instead of dividing (the current ratio is inverted relative to the voltage ratio); 2 A ignores the transformer; 0.005 A divides by the square of the turns ratio, which is the rule for referring impedances, not currents.

questions.q: A single-phase load draws 5 A rms from a 230 V rms supply at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. Find the apparent, real and reactive power, and state whether the load is inductive or capacitive.
markScheme: Q = √(S² − P²) = 690 var (or S sin φ with sin φ = 0.6)
Lagging power factor means current lags voltage: inductive load
questions.modelAnswer: Apparent power S = VI = 230 × 5 = 1150 VA. With cos φ = 0.8, real power P = 1150 × 0.8 = 920 W. Since sin φ = √(1 − 0.8²) = 0.6, reactive power Q = 1150 × 0.6 = 690 var (check: 920² + 690² = 1150²). A lagging power factor means the current lags the voltage, so the load is inductive.
